## The candidate comparison

Cañete, Miranda Jr., and Vittone study the planar isoperimetric problem with density

\[
f_\lambda(x)=\begin{cases}
\lambda,&|x|\leq 1,\\
1,&|x|>1,
\end{cases}
\qquad 0<\lambda<1.
\]

Weighted area is the integral of this density over a region; weighted perimeter uses the same density on its boundary. In particular, an arc on the unit circle has weight \(\lambda\). The relevant candidates are regions of type (B), bounded by an arc of the unit circle and an exterior circular arc meeting it at angle \(\arccos\lambda\), and balls of type (C), whose boundaries meet the unit circle orthogonally. The source classification and candidate formulas are in [CMV, Proposition 3.22, pp. 32–33, and Theorem 3.23, pp. 34–36]. We prove an analytic comparison of these two complete candidate families. Its application to arbitrary finite-perimeter minimizers requires the source-level geometric premises discussed at the end.

For a weighted area \(v\), let \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm B}(v)\) and \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm C}(v)\) be the sets of weighted perimeters of all admissible candidates of the indicated type having area exactly \(v\), and define

\[
I_{\mathrm B}(v)=\inf\mathcal P_{\mathrm B}(v),
\qquad I_{\mathrm C}(v)=\inf\mathcal P_{\mathrm C}(v).
\]

The admissible parameter domains and formulas are specified below. On the domain \(v>\lambda\pi\) used here, both sets are nonempty singletons; thus these definitions neither select a favorable branch nor depend on the value assigned to an empty infimum. [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBPerimeterValuesAtArea] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCPerimeterValuesAtArea] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBPerimeterAtArea] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCPerimeterAtArea] [@lean:CMVBallCase.exists_typeBRadius_at_area] [@lean:CMVBallCase.exists_typeCRadius_at_area] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBPerimeterAtArea_eq_radius] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCPerimeterAtArea_eq_radius]

**Theorem.** Let \(0<\lambda<1\) and \(\lambda\pi<v_0<v\). If

\[
I_{\mathrm C}(v_0)\leq I_{\mathrm B}(v_0),
\]

then

\[
I_{\mathrm C}(v)<I_{\mathrm B}(v).
\]

Thus weak dominance of type (C) at one such area becomes strict dominance at every larger area. This is the formal persistence theorem, not an unconditional classification of isoperimetric regions. [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeC_dominance_persists]

## Candidate formulas and global parameters

Fix \(0<\lambda<1\) throughout the proof, and put

\[
a=\arccos\lambda,\qquad s=\sqrt{1-\lambda^2},\qquad
S(t)=t-\sin t\cos t.
\]

For a unit circle, \(S(t)\) is the area of the circular segment with central angle \(2t\), for \(0\leq t\leq\pi\). For type (B), take

\[
0<\beta\leq\pi-a,\qquad \alpha=\beta+a,\qquad
r=\frac{\sin\alpha}{\sin\beta}.
\]

The two boundary arcs have lengths \(2r(\pi-\beta)\) and \(2\alpha\). The region contains the unit disk. Its Euclidean area is the sum of the two circular segments cut by their common chord; subtracting \((1-\lambda)\pi\) gives its weighted area. Consequently the formulas in [CMV, p. 34, Figure 19 on p. 35] are

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf P_{\mathrm B}(\beta)&=2\bigl((\pi-\beta)r+\lambda\alpha\bigr),\\
\mathsf A_{\mathrm B}(\beta)&=r^2\bigl(\pi-\beta+\sin\beta\cos\beta\bigr)
 +S(\alpha)-(1-\lambda)\pi.
\end{aligned}
\]

The endpoint \(\beta=\pi-a\) is retained: it has \(r=0\) and represents the unit disk. The endpoint \(\beta=0\) printed in the source is an infinite-radius limit, not a finite candidate. [@lean:CMVBallCase.BAdmissible] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBAlpha] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBRadius] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBPerimeter] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBArea] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBRadius_endpoint_zero] [@lean:CMVBallCase.arcSegment]

For type (C), let \(0<b<\pi/2\), and set \(R=\cot b\). The inner and outer boundary arcs have lengths \(2Rb\) and \(2R(\pi-b)\). Orthogonality gives an overlap with the unit disk consisting of segments of areas \(R^2S(b)\) and \(S(\pi/2-b)\). Hence [CMV, p. 35]

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf P_{\mathrm C}(b)&=2R\bigl(\pi-(1-\lambda)b\bigr),\\
\mathsf A_{\mathrm C}(b)&=R^2\bigl(\pi-(1-\lambda)S(b)\bigr)
 -(1-\lambda)S(\pi/2-b).
\end{aligned}
\]

These are exactly the source's formulas with \(R=1/\tan b\). Both angular endpoints are excluded degenerations. The elementary geometric descriptions explain the formulas; the formal objects are the explicit real-valued formulas, not sets equipped with a formalized perimeter measure. [@lean:CMVBallCase.CAdmissible] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCRadius] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCPerimeter] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCArea]

Use radius as a global parameter. The identity and inverse charts are

\[
r=\lambda+s\cot\beta,\qquad
\beta_\lambda(R)=\frac\pi2-\arctan\frac{R-\lambda}{s},\qquad
b(R)=\arctan\frac1R.
\]

The first chart is a bijection between the finite type-(B) angle domain and \(R\geq0\); the second is a bijection between \(0<b<\pi/2\) and \(R>0\). The radius maps are strictly decreasing in their angle parameters, and the displayed inverses work on their entire domains. In particular, the type-(B) chart includes \(R<\lambda\), where \(\beta_\lambda(R)>\pi/2\), as well as \(R\geq\lambda\); no quadrant is discarded. [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBRadius_eq_add_sqrt_mul_cot] [@lean:CMVBallCase.betaAtRadius] [@lean:CMVBallCase.bAtRadius] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBRadius_strictAntiOn] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCRadius_strictAntiOn] [@lean:CMVBallCase.betaAtRadius_admissible] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBRadius_betaAtRadius] [@lean:CMVBallCase.betaAtRadius_typeBRadius] [@lean:CMVBallCase.bAtRadius_admissible] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCRadius_bAtRadius] [@lean:CMVBallCase.bAtRadius_typeCRadius]

Write \(P_{\mathrm B}(R),A_{\mathrm B}(R)\) for the type-(B) formulas evaluated at \(\beta_\lambda(R)\), and \(P_{\mathrm C}(R),A_{\mathrm C}(R)\) for the type-(C) formulas evaluated at \(b(R)\). Thus

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_{\mathrm B}(R)&=2\bigl((\pi-\beta_\lambda(R))R+\lambda(\beta_\lambda(R)+a)\bigr),\\
A_{\mathrm B}(R)&=R^2\bigl(\pi-S(\beta_\lambda(R))\bigr)
 +S(\beta_\lambda(R)+a)-(1-\lambda)\pi,\\
P_{\mathrm C}(R)&=2R\bigl(\pi-(1-\lambda)b(R)\bigr),\\
A_{\mathrm C}(R)&=R^2\bigl(\pi-(1-\lambda)S(b(R))\bigr)
 -(1-\lambda)S(\pi/2-b(R)).
\end{aligned}
\]

The radius formulas agree with the angular formulas for every admissible radius. ## Area and perimeter monotonicity

Differentiation, using \(S'(t)=2\sin^2t\), gives, for \(R>0\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_{\mathrm B}'(R)&=2\bigl(\pi-S(\beta_\lambda(R))\bigr),
& A_{\mathrm B}'(R)&=R P_{\mathrm B}'(R),\\
P_{\mathrm C}'(R)&=2\bigl(\pi-(1-\lambda)S(b(R))\bigr),
& A_{\mathrm C}'(R)&=R P_{\mathrm C}'(R).
\end{aligned}
\]

Both perimeter derivatives are positive. Indeed, the first factor is \(S(\pi-\beta_\lambda(R))>0\), while \(0<S(b(R))<b(R)<\pi/2\) makes the second factor positive. Thus area and perimeter are strictly increasing in radius: on \([0,\infty)\) for type (B), and on \((0,\infty)\) for type (C). Continuity at the type-(B) endpoint supplies the closed endpoint assertion. [@lean:CMVBallCase.arcSegment_hasDerivAt] [@lean:CMVBallCase.arcSegment_pos] [@lean:CMVBallCase.arcSegment_lt_self] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBPerimeterAtRadius_hasDerivAt] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCPerimeterAtRadius_hasDerivAt] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBAreaAtRadius_hasDerivAt] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCAreaAtRadius_hasDerivAt] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeB_perimeter_factor_pos] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeC_perimeter_factor_pos] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBAreaAtRadius_strictMonoOn] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCAreaAtRadius_strictMonoOn] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBPerimeterAtRadius_strictMonoOn] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCPerimeterAtRadius_strictMonoOn]

The relevant area ranges follow without an arbitrary inverse choice. For type (B),

\[
A_{\mathrm B}(0)=\lambda\pi,\qquad P_{\mathrm B}(0)=2\lambda\pi,\qquad
A_{\mathrm B}(R)>\frac\pi2R^2-\pi\quad(R\geq\lambda).
\]

For type (C), the useful bounds are

\[
\lambda\pi R^2-\frac\pi2<A_{\mathrm C}(R)<\pi R^2\quad(R>0).
\]

In particular, \(A_{\mathrm C}(\lambda)<\pi\lambda^2<\lambda\pi\), and its lower bound tends to infinity. The intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity therefore give a unique positive radius of each type at every area \(v>\lambda\pi\). The inverse angle charts show that every admissible angular candidate of that area has this radius and this angle. Consequently the all-candidate perimeter sets are singletons and the infima are their actual perimeter values. Moreover, \(I_{\mathrm B}\) is strictly increasing on \((\lambda\pi,\infty)\), and \(I_{\mathrm B}(v)>2\lambda\pi\) there. ## The fixed-radius comparison

We next prove the decisive inequality

\[
P_{\mathrm C}(R)<P_{\mathrm B}(R)\qquad(R>0).
\]

This is a comparison at equal radii, not at equal areas. Half the perimeter difference is

\[
H(\lambda,R)=(\lambda-R)\beta_\lambda(R)
 +\lambda\arccos\lambda+(1-\lambda)R b(R).
\]

For \(0<R\leq\lambda\), the first term is nonnegative and the other two are positive, so \(H(\lambda,R)>0\). [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusHalfGap] [@lean:CMVBallCase.perimeter_gap_eq_two_mul_halfGap] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusHalfGap_pos_of_le]

For the remaining region \(R>\lambda\), vary the density while keeping \(R\) fixed. For \(0<c<1\), define

\[
\begin{aligned}
D(c,R)&=(R-c)^2+1-c^2,\\
L(c,R)&=\beta_c(R)-b(R)-\frac{c\sqrt{1-c^2}}{D(c,R)},\\
N(c,R)&=R^3-4R^2c+2Rc^2+3R-2c.
\end{aligned}
\]

Here \(D(c,R)>0\), and direct differentiation yields

\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial c}\frac{H(c,R)}c=\frac R{c^2}L(c,R),
\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial c}(c,R)=
-\frac{cN(c,R)}{\sqrt{1-c^2}D(c,R)^2}.
\]

The polynomial has the particularly useful derivative and diagonal value

\[
\frac{\partial N}{\partial c}(c,R)=
-\bigl(4(R-\tfrac12)^2+1+4R(1-c)\bigr)<0
\quad(R>0,\ c<1),
\qquad N(R,R)=R(1-R^2).
\]

Thus \(N(\cdot,R)\) is strictly decreasing on \(( -\infty,1]\). [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusD] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusL] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusN] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusD_pos] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusHalfGap_density_ratio_hasDerivAt] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusL_density_hasDerivAt] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusN_density_derivative_identity] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusN_density_derivative_neg] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusN_diagonal] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusN_strictAntiOn]

We claim \(L(c,R)<0\) for \(0<c<\min(1,R)\). First, \(L(0,R)=0\), and \(L(\cdot,R)\) is continuous at zero. If \(N(c,R)\geq0\), then \(N(t,R)>0\) for \(0<t<c\). Hence \(L\) strictly decreases from zero on \([0,c]\), proving the claim, including the case \(N(c,R)=0\). If \(R\leq1\), this case always applies, because

\[
N(c,R)>N(R,R)=R(1-R^2)\geq0.
\]

If instead \(N(c,R)<0\), necessarily \(R>1\). For every \(c<t<1\), we have \(N(t,R)<0\), so \(L\) is strictly increasing to its left limit at one. The reciprocal angle formula

\[
\beta_t(R)=\arctan\frac{\sqrt{1-t^2}}{R-t}\qquad(t<R)
\]

shows that this limit is \(-b(R)<0\). Therefore \(L(c,R)\leq-b(R)<0\) in this case as well. The restriction \(c<R\) is essential to this argument. [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusL_zero] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusL_continuousAt_zero] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusL_neg_of_N_nonneg] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusN_pos_of_radius_le_one] [@lean:CMVBallCase.betaAtRadius_eq_arctan_reciprocal] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusL_tendsto_one] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusL_neg_of_N_neg] [@lean:CMVBallCase.fixedRadiusL_neg]

It follows that \(H(c,R)/c\) is strictly decreasing for \(0<c<\min(1,R)\). If \(\lambda<R<1\), continuity at \(c=R\) and the already proved case of equal density and radius give

\[
\frac{H(\lambda,R)}\lambda>\frac{H(R,R)}R>0.
\]

If \(R\geq1\), then

\[
\lim_{c\uparrow1}\frac{H(c,R)}c=0.
\]

For \(R>1\) this follows from the reciprocal angle formula. For \(R=1\), the bound \(0<\beta_c(1)\leq\pi/2\) makes \((1-c)\beta_c(1)\to0\), while the remaining terms tend to zero. Strict decrease and this limit imply \(H(\lambda,R)/\lambda>0\): choose an intermediate density \(\lambda<c<1\), whose ratio is nonnegative by the limit, and compare strictly with it. Together with the case \(R\leq\lambda\), this proves the fixed-radius inequality for every \(R>0\). ## Common perimeter and persistence

For \(p>2\lambda\pi\), let \(r_{\mathrm B}(p)\) and \(r_{\mathrm C}(p)\) be the unique positive radii satisfying

\[
P_{\mathrm B}(r_{\mathrm B}(p))=p,\qquad
P_{\mathrm C}(r_{\mathrm C}(p))=p.
\]

To see existence, note that \(P_{\mathrm B}(0)=2\lambda\pi\), \(P_{\mathrm C}(\lambda)<2\lambda\pi\), and

\[
\pi R<P_{\mathrm C}(R)<P_{\mathrm B}(R)\qquad(R>0).
\]

Continuity supplies the required radii, and strict monotonicity supplies uniqueness. The same-radius comparison then implies

\[
r_{\mathrm B}(p)<r_{\mathrm C}(p):
\]

otherwise monotonicity of \(P_{\mathrm C}\) would give \(p\leq P_{\mathrm C}(r_{\mathrm B}(p))<p\). These inverses are used only on the genuine open common-perimeter domain. [@lean:CMVBallCase.CommonPerimeter] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCPerimeterAtRadius_gt_pi_mul_radius] [@lean:CMVBallCase.existsUnique_typeBRadius_at_perimeter] [@lean:CMVBallCase.existsUnique_typeCRadius_at_perimeter] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBRadiusAtPerimeter] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCRadiusAtPerimeter] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBRadiusAtPerimeter_lt_typeCRadiusAtPerimeter]

Define the area difference at common perimeter by

\[
G(p)=A_{\mathrm B}(r_{\mathrm B}(p))
      -A_{\mathrm C}(r_{\mathrm C}(p)).
\]

The perimeter derivatives are continuous and positive at positive radii, so the one-dimensional inverse function theorem applies locally. Using \(A_{\mathrm B}'=R P_{\mathrm B}'\) and \(A_{\mathrm C}'=R P_{\mathrm C}'\), the chain rule gives

\[
\frac{d}{dp}A_{\mathrm B}(r_{\mathrm B}(p))=r_{\mathrm B}(p),\qquad
\frac{d}{dp}A_{\mathrm C}(r_{\mathrm C}(p))=r_{\mathrm C}(p).
\]

Consequently

\[
G'(p)=r_{\mathrm B}(p)-r_{\mathrm C}(p)<0.
\]

The mean value theorem on each compact subinterval of \((2\lambda\pi,\infty)\) makes \(G\) strictly decreasing throughout that domain. This is the monotone quantity used in the proof; no monotonicity of \(I_{\mathrm B}-I_{\mathrm C}\) is assumed. [@lean:CMVBallCase.commonPerimeterAreaGap] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeBPerimeterAtRadius_hasStrictDerivAt] [@lean:CMVBallCase.typeCPerimeterAtRadius_hasStrictDerivAt] [@lean:CMVBallCase.commonPerimeterAreaGap_local_hasDerivAt] [@lean:CMVBallCase.commonPerimeterAreaGap_strictAnti]

Now suppose \(\lambda\pi<v_0<v\) and \(I_{\mathrm C}(v_0)\leq I_{\mathrm B}(v_0)\). Put \(p_0=I_{\mathrm B}(v_0)\). At this perimeter the type-(B) area is \(v_0\). The type-(C) radius realizing area \(v_0\) has perimeter at most \(p_0\), so monotonicity of its perimeter and area maps gives

\[
A_{\mathrm C}(r_{\mathrm C}(p_0))\geq v_0,\qquad G(p_0)\leq0.
\]

Because \(I_{\mathrm B}\) is strictly increasing, \(p=I_{\mathrm B}(v)>p_0\). Hence

\[
G(p)<G(p_0)\leq0,\qquad
A_{\mathrm C}(r_{\mathrm C}(p))>v.
\]

The unique type-(C) radius of area \(v\) is therefore strictly less than \(r_{\mathrm C}(p)\); its perimeter is strictly less than \(p=I_{\mathrm B}(v)\). This proves the theorem. ## Geometric scope

The verified result is persistence of type-(C) dominance over the faithful all-candidate type-(B)/(C) profiles. The formal argument establishes the full finite parameter domains, equality with the source formulas, existence and uniqueness at the required areas and perimeters, and the strict common-perimeter comparison. It does not itself establish existence or regularity of finite-perimeter minimizers, their connectedness, or the exhaustiveness of the geometric candidate classification. Nor does the persistence implication alone assert that a crossing exists.

The paper-level conclusion \(v_1=v_2\), proposed in the remark after [CMV, Theorem 3.23, p. 34], follows only when this analytic theorem is combined with the finite-perimeter existence, regularity, connectedness, and exhaustive candidate-classification premises underlying Proposition 3.22 and Theorem 3.23, together with the latter theorem's small- and large-area alternatives. Under those external premises, above \(\lambda\pi\) every minimizer is of type (B) or (C), type (B) wins near that endpoint, and type (C) wins for sufficiently large areas. The continuous candidate profiles therefore meet; at their meeting both types are optimal, and persistence excludes any later return of type (B). Thus the transition thresholds can be taken equal. These geometric-measure-theory premises and this global minimizer classification are not formalized in this package; they are distinct from the verified analytic profile theorem.

supplement_introduction:
The entries give the mathematical content of each declaration in the publication closure. Declarations classified as main support the conventional proof; supplement entries record the elementary trigonometric identities, algebra, continuity facts, and domain-transport details used to implement it. Each entry states its mathematical hypotheses and conclusion separately from the source metadata and Lean code supplied with it. There are no configured generated families and no generated declarations in this inventory, so no family representatives or computational certificate ledger are required.

Use the main proof's notation: \(S(t)=t-\sin t\cos t\), \(a=\arccos\lambda\), \(s=\sqrt{1-\lambda^2}\), \(\beta_\lambda(R)=\pi/2-\arctan((R-\lambda)/s)\), and \(b(R)=\arctan(1/R)\). Angular area and perimeter functions are denoted by \(\mathsf A,\mathsf P\); their radius versions by \(A,P\); and the equal-area profiles by \(I\). Write \(Q_{\mathrm B}(R)=\pi-S(\beta_\lambda(R))\) and \(Q_{\mathrm C}(R)=\pi-(1-\lambda)S(b(R))\). The functions \(H,D,L,N\), common-perimeter inverses \(r_{\mathrm B},r_{\mathrm C}\), and area difference \(G\) are those defined in the main proof. Density dependence is suppressed in this notation except when density is the differentiation variable.

The formulas are total real-valued expressions in the source, but their geometric interpretation is restricted to the stated admissible domains. In particular, no geometric meaning is assigned here to a totalized division at an excluded endpoint. A derivative described as strict is the two-point derivative limit used by the inverse function theorem; it is not an assertion that the derivative is strictly positive. Common-perimeter inverses are defined only for \(p>2\lambda\pi\). The auxiliary clamping operation merely realizes their area difference as an ordinary real function on a fixed upper interval. It does not change a candidate family or extend an inverse to an inadmissible perimeter. The supplement supplies analytic details, not the unformalized geometric classification discussed at the close of the main proof.

classifications.informal_statement: A type-(B) angle is admissible precisely when 0 < β ≤ π − arccos λ.
classifications.latex_explanation: The predicate is \(0<\beta\land\beta\leq\pi-\arccos\lambda\). For \(0<\lambda<1\) it retains the zero-radius endpoint and excludes the infinite-radius limit \(\beta=0\). The predicate itself does not impose the density hypothesis.

classifications.informal_statement: A type-(C) angle is admissible precisely when 0 < β < π/2.
classifications.latex_explanation: The domain is the open interval \((0,\pi/2)\). Its endpoints correspond to infinite and zero radius, respectively, and neither is a finite positive-radius candidate.

classifications.informal_statement: Every admissible type-(C) angle has positive radius.
classifications.latex_explanation: For \(0<\beta<\pi/2\), \(\tan\beta>0\), hence \(1/\tan\beta>0\). This places every angular candidate in the positive radius chart.

classifications.informal_statement: The type-(C) radius is strictly decreasing on (0, π/2).
classifications.latex_explanation: If \(0<\beta<\beta'<\pi/2\), then \(1/\tan\beta'>0\) and \(1/\tan\beta'<1/\tan\beta\). Strict increase of tangent and positivity justify taking reciprocals.

classifications.informal_statement: Two admissible type-(C) angles with equal radii are equal.
classifications.latex_explanation: The restriction \(\beta\mapsto\cot\beta\) to \((0,\pi/2)\) is injective by strict decrease. Thus no second angular branch can have the same positive radius.

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < 1, then √(1 − λ²) > 0.
classifications.latex_explanation: The density hypotheses give \(1-\lambda^2>0\). Taking its nonnegative square root gives a strictly positive coefficient, allowing division in the type-(B) chart.

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1, the square of √(1 − λ²) is 1 − λ².
classifications.latex_explanation: The identity \(s^2=1-\lambda^2\) follows from nonnegativity of the radicand. It is used to simplify rational derivative formulas without changing their domains.

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1 and an admissible type-(B) angle β, sin β > 0.
classifications.latex_explanation: Since \(0<\arccos\lambda\), admissibility implies \(0<\beta<\pi\). Hence \(\sin\beta>0\), so the defining radius quotient has a nonzero denominator.

classifications.informal_statement: For every BAdmissible λ β, sin(β + arccos λ) is nonnegative.
classifications.latex_explanation: No separate density assumption is required: admissibility and \(\arccos\lambda\geq0\) put \(\alpha=\beta+\arccos\lambda\) in \([0,\pi]\). Its sine is nonnegative, including the endpoint \(\alpha=\pi\).

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1 and admissible β, the type-(B) radius equals λ + √(1 − λ²) cot β.
classifications.latex_explanation: Expanding \(\sin(\beta+\arccos\lambda)\) and dividing by the positive \(\sin\beta\) gives \(r=\lambda+s\cot\beta\). This identity supplies a global inverse without a quadrant-dependent inverse tangent.

classifications.informal_statement: Cotangent is strictly decreasing on (0, π).
classifications.latex_explanation: For \(0<x<y<\pi\), \(\cot y<\cot x\). The proof uses \(\cot x=\tan(\pi/2-x)\) and strict increase of tangent on \((-\pi/2,\pi/2)\).

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1, the type-(B) radius is strictly decreasing on its whole admissible angular domain.
classifications.latex_explanation: On \(0<\beta\leq\pi-a\), \(r=\lambda+s\cot\beta\) with \(s>0\). Strict decrease of cotangent gives strict decrease of radius, including comparisons with the zero-radius endpoint.

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1, equal radii of admissible type-(B) angles imply equal angles.
classifications.latex_explanation: Injectivity follows from strict decrease on \((0,\pi-a]\). This is the uniqueness statement needed to recover every angular candidate from the global radius chart.

classifications.informal_statement: The type-(B) inverse chart is βλ(R) = π/2 − arctan((R − λ)/√(1 − λ²)).
classifications.latex_explanation: The formula is defined for all real inputs as a total real expression. Its inverse-chart interpretation uses \(0<\lambda<1\) and \(R\geq0\); it covers angles on both sides of \(\pi/2\).

classifications.informal_statement: For every R > 0, L(0,R) = 0.
classifications.latex_explanation: The correction term vanishes and \(\pi/2-\arctan R=\arctan(1/R)=b(R)\). This zero-density endpoint anchors the decreasing part of the sign argument.

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < 1 and λ < R, then βλ(R) = arctan(√(1 − λ²)/(R − λ)).
classifications.latex_explanation: The argument \((R-\lambda)/s\) is positive, so the complementary arctangent identity applies. The restriction \(R>\lambda\) prevents using this acute-angle chart in the other quadrant.

classifications.informal_statement: For R > 0, the function c ↦ L(c,R) is continuous at c = 0.
classifications.latex_explanation: At zero density the square-root denominator is one and \(D(0,R)=R^2+1>0\). Ordinary continuity rules therefore apply, justifying comparison with \(L(0,R)=0\).

classifications.informal_statement: For R > 1, L(c,R) tends to −b(R) as c tends to 1 from below.
classifications.latex_explanation: The reciprocal chart gives \(\beta_c(R)\to0\), while \(c\sqrt{1-c^2}/D(c,R)\to0\) because \(D(1,R)=(R-1)^2>0\). The claim deliberately excludes \(R=1\).

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < 1, λ < R, and N(λ,R) ≥ 0, then L(λ,R) < 0.
classifications.latex_explanation: Strict decrease of \(N(\cdot,R)\) gives \(N(c,R)>0\) for \(0<c<\lambda\), even when \(N(\lambda,R)=0\). Hence \(L\) strictly decreases from its continuous zero value on \([0,\lambda]\).

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < R ≤ 1, then N(λ,R) > 0.
classifications.latex_explanation: Strict density decrease gives \(N(\lambda,R)>N(R,R)\). The diagonal identity makes the latter \(R(1-R^2)\geq0\), including \(R=1\).

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < 1 < R and N(λ,R) < 0, then L(λ,R) < 0.
classifications.latex_explanation: For \(\lambda<c<1\), the polynomial remains negative, so \(L\) increases on \([\lambda,1)\). Its left limit is \(-b(R)<0\); therefore \(L(\lambda,R)\leq-b(R)<0\).

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < 1 and λ < R, then L(λ,R) < 0.
classifications.latex_explanation: For \(R\leq1\), positivity of \(N\) applies. For \(R>1\), split according to \(N\geq0\) or \(N<0\), using the zero-density or unit-density endpoint respectively. No sign is claimed outside \(R>\lambda\).

classifications.informal_statement: For R > 0, c ↦ H(c,R)/c is strictly decreasing on (0, min(1,R)).
classifications.latex_explanation: On that interval, \(L(c,R)<0\) and \(R/c^2>0\). The ratio derivative is therefore strictly negative everywhere, and the mean value theorem yields strict decrease.

classifications.informal_statement: For any real R and 0 < c < 1, the function x ↦ H(x,R)/x is continuous at c.
classifications.latex_explanation: Its established density derivative implies continuity. In particular, for \(0<R<1\), this allows comparison with the finite endpoint \(c=R\) of the decreasing interval.

classifications.informal_statement: For R > 1, H(c,R)/c tends to zero as c tends to 1 from below.
classifications.latex_explanation: Use the reciprocal chart: \(\beta_c(R)\to0\), \(\arccos c\to0\), and \(1-c\to0\), while \(c\to1\). Every term in the quotient therefore tends to zero.

classifications.informal_statement: H(c,1)/c tends to zero as c tends to 1 from below.
classifications.latex_explanation: At this corner, bound \(0\leq(1-c)\beta_c(1)\leq(1-c)\pi/2\). This product tends to zero without assigning an endpoint angle to the singular chart; the arccosine and remaining weighted term also vanish.

classifications.informal_statement: For every R ≥ 1, H(c,R)/c tends to zero as c tends to 1 from below.
classifications.latex_explanation: The proof separates \(R=1\), handled by a squeeze estimate, from \(R>1\), handled by the reciprocal chart. This is a pointwise limit for each radius, with no uniform-radius assertion.

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < R < 1, then H(λ,R) > 0.
classifications.latex_explanation: The ratio extends continuously to \(c=R\) and is strictly decreasing on \((0,R]\). Hence \(H(\lambda,R)/\lambda>H(R,R)/R>0\), where the endpoint positivity comes from the direct \(R\leq c\) case.

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < 1 and R ≥ 1, then H(λ,R) > 0.
classifications.latex_explanation: The ratio strictly decreases on \((0,1)\) and tends to zero at one. Comparing \(\lambda\) with any larger interior density, whose ratio is nonnegative by the endpoint limit, yields strict positivity at \(\lambda\).

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < 1 and R > λ, then H(λ,R) > 0.
classifications.latex_explanation: Split into \(R<1\) and \(R\geq1\). The finite diagonal comparison and the unit-density limit, respectively, cover all radii in this region, including radii arbitrarily close to \(\lambda\).

classifications.informal_statement: For every 0 < λ < 1 and R > 0, P_C(R) < P_B(R).
classifications.latex_explanation: The identity \(P_{\mathrm B}(R)-P_{\mathrm C}(R)=2H(\lambda,R)\) reduces the conclusion to positivity of \(H\). The cases \(R\leq\lambda\) and \(R>\lambda\) prove it over the complete positive radius domain.

classifications.informal_statement: For a real λ, CommonPerimeter λ is the set of real p with p > 2λπ, regarded as a domain of arguments.
classifications.latex_explanation: The domain is \(J_\lambda=(2\lambda\pi,\infty)\). Packaging the inequality with \(p\) ensures that inverse radii are defined only where both positive-radius perimeter equations are proved solvable.

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < 1 and R > 0, then P_C(R) > πR.
classifications.latex_explanation: Since \((1-\lambda)b(R)<\pi/2\), the factor \(\pi-(1-\lambda)b(R)\) is greater than \(\pi/2\). Multiplication by \(2R>0\) gives the bound and proves unbounded perimeter growth.

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1 and p > 2λπ, there is exactly one R with R > 0 and P_B(R) = p.
classifications.latex_explanation: Start with \(P_{\mathrm B}(0)=2\lambda\pi<p\), and use \(P_{\mathrm B}(R)>P_{\mathrm C}(R)>\pi R\) at a large radius. Continuity gives existence and strict perimeter increase gives uniqueness among positive radii.

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1 and p > 2λπ, there is exactly one R with R > 0 and P_C(R) = p.
classifications.latex_explanation: The radius \(R=\lambda\) has perimeter less than \(2\lambda\pi\); sufficiently large radii have perimeter greater than \(p\). The intermediate value theorem and strict increase give existence and uniqueness without evaluating at radius zero.

classifications.informal_statement: For an admissible density and p > 2λπ, r_B(p) is the unique positive radius with P_B(r_B(p)) = p.
classifications.latex_explanation: The source chooses the witness from the proved existence-and-uniqueness theorem and retains its positivity and perimeter equation as part of the value. No inverse value is specified at or below the endpoint.

classifications.informal_statement: For an admissible density and p > 2λπ, r_C(p) is the unique positive radius with P_C(r_C(p)) = p.
classifications.latex_explanation: The definition selects the uniquely characterized positive solution and carries its defining equation. The use of choice here does not choose among competing geometric branches, since uniqueness has already been proved.

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1 and p > 2λπ, r_B(p) > 0.
classifications.latex_explanation: This extracts the positivity already contained in the inverse radius definition. It permits applying derivative and monotonicity results on the positive radius chart.

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1 and p > 2λπ, r_C(p) > 0.
classifications.latex_explanation: Positivity is part of the defining characterization of the chosen inverse. The lemma exposes it for subsequent uses of the positive-radius analytic formulas.

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1 and p > 2λπ, P_B(r_B(p)) = p.
classifications.latex_explanation: This is the defining perimeter equation of the inverse, extracted from its stored characterization. It is an exact equality at a genuine common perimeter.

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1 and p > 2λπ, P_C(r_C(p)) = p.
classifications.latex_explanation: The equation is supplied by the existence theorem used to define \(r_{\mathrm C}\). It identifies the actual perimeter of the radius selected by the inverse.

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < 1, p > 2λπ, R > 0, and P_B(R) = p, then r_B(p) = R.
classifications.latex_explanation: Both radii solve the same positive-radius perimeter equation. Uniqueness identifies the chosen global inverse with any local inverse or explicit positive candidate satisfying that equation.

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < 1, p > 2λπ, R > 0, and P_C(R) = p, then r_C(p) = R.
classifications.latex_explanation: This is uniqueness of the positive solution at perimeter \(p\). It is used to identify the local inverse supplied by calculus with the genuine common-perimeter inverse.

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1 and p > 2λπ, r_B(p) < r_C(p).
classifications.latex_explanation: If \(r_{\mathrm C}(p)\leq r_{\mathrm B}(p)\), monotonicity and the equal-radius comparison would give \(p=P_{\mathrm C}(r_{\mathrm C}(p))\leq P_{\mathrm C}(r_{\mathrm B}(p))<P_{\mathrm B}(r_{\mathrm B}(p))=p\). This contradiction proves strict radius order.

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1 and every real R, P_B has strict derivative 2Q_B(R) at R.
classifications.latex_explanation: The two-point quotient \((P_{\mathrm B}(x)-P_{\mathrm B}(y))/(x-y)\) tends to \(2Q_{\mathrm B}(R)\) as distinct \(x,y\to R\). The ordinary derivative formula is continuous, so strict differentiability follows; at positive radii its nonzero value allows local inversion.

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1 and R > 0, P_C has strict derivative 2Q_C(R) at R.
classifications.latex_explanation: The derivative formula is continuous in a neighborhood of every positive radius. Therefore the two-point derivative limit holds, providing the strict differentiability required by the inverse function theorem.

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1 and p > 2λπ, G(p) is A_B(r_B(p)) − A_C(r_C(p)).
classifications.latex_explanation: Both radii realize the same genuine perimeter \(p\). The gap is defined on this open perimeter domain, not on all real perimeters and not as a difference of equal-area profiles.

classifications.informal_statement: For an admissible density and each p > 2λπ, there is a real function agreeing locally with G on its domain and having derivative r_B(p) − r_C(p) at p.
classifications.latex_explanation: The statement supplies \(g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) with \(g'(p)=r_{\mathrm B}(p)-r_{\mathrm C}(p)\), and a neighborhood of \(p\) where \(g(q)=G(q)\) for every \(q>2\lambda\pi\). Local inverse derivatives and \(A'=RP'\) give the formula; no global off-domain inverse is introduced.

classifications.informal_statement: For p > 2λπ and real q, the clamped common perimeter is max(q,p).
classifications.latex_explanation: The value \(\max(q,p)\) remains strictly above \(2\lambda\pi\). This transports a function on the constrained perimeter domain to an ordinary real argument for interval calculus.

classifications.informal_statement: If p > 2λπ and q ≥ p, clamping q at p leaves q unchanged.
classifications.latex_explanation: The equality \(\max(q,p)=q\) holds under \(p\leq q\). It also identifies the corresponding constrained-domain values, so clamping does not alter the gap anywhere on the interval used by the mean value theorem.

classifications.informal_statement: For an admissible density and p > 2λπ, the real function G_p(q) is G(max(q,p)).
classifications.latex_explanation: The definition is a constant extension below \(p\) and agrees with \(G\) for \(q\geq p\). Only its restriction to that upper interval is used; it does not assign inverse radii to inadmissible perimeters.

classifications.informal_statement: For 0 < λ < 1, p > 2λπ, and q ≥ p, G_p has derivative within [p,∞) equal to r_B(q) − r_C(q).
classifications.latex_explanation: Local agreement with a differentiable representative of \(G\) proves the derivative relative to \([p,\infty)\). At \(q=p\) this is a one-sided derivative, not a claim of ordinary differentiability across the clamping point.

classifications.informal_statement: For every 0 < λ < 1, G is strictly decreasing on the common-perimeter domain (2λπ,∞).
classifications.latex_explanation: For \(2\lambda\pi<p<q\), use the continuous clamped representative on \([p,q]\). Its interior derivative is \(r_{\mathrm B}-r_{\mathrm C}<0\), so the mean value theorem gives \(G(q)<G(p)\).

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < 1 and v > λπ, then I_B(v) > 2λπ.
classifications.latex_explanation: The type-(B) area \(v\) is realized at a positive radius. Strict perimeter increase from \(P_{\mathrm B}(0)=2\lambda\pi\) makes its profile perimeter a valid argument of the common-perimeter gap.

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < 1, v > λπ, and I_C(v) ≤ I_B(v), then G(I_B(v)) ≤ 0.
classifications.latex_explanation: At \(p=I_{\mathrm B}(v)\), the type-(B) area is \(v\). The type-(C) area radius has perimeter at most \(p\), hence is at most \(r_{\mathrm C}(p)\). Area monotonicity gives \(A_{\mathrm C}(r_{\mathrm C}(p))\geq v\), so the B-minus-C gap is nonpositive.

classifications.informal_statement: If 0 < λ < 1, v > λπ, and G(I_B(v)) < 0, then I_C(v) < I_B(v).
classifications.latex_explanation: At \(p=I_{\mathrm B}(v)\), negativity says \(A_{\mathrm C}(r_{\mathrm C}(p))>v\). The unique type-(C) radius of area \(v\) is strictly smaller, so its strictly increasing perimeter is less than \(p\).

classifications.informal_statement: For all real λ, v₀, v with 0 < λ < 1 and λπ < v₀ < v, I_C(v₀) ≤ I_B(v₀) implies I_C(v) < I_B(v).
classifications.latex_explanation: Set \(p_0=I_{\mathrm B}(v_0)\) and \(p=I_{\mathrm B}(v)\). Strict profile increase gives \(p_0<p\), initial dominance gives \(G(p_0)\leq0\), and strict gap decrease gives \(G(p)<0\). The final bridge yields strict type-(C) dominance. This is the exact primary root and has no hypothesis asserting geometric classification or prior strict dominance.

classifications.informal_statement: An admissible density parameter is a real λ satisfying 0 < λ and λ < 1.
classifications.latex_explanation: The predicate abbreviates exactly \(0<\lambda<1\). It excludes both constant-density endpoints and adds no condition about candidate optimality or minimizer classification.

classifications.informal_statement: The type-(B) auxiliary angle is α = β + arccos λ.
classifications.latex_explanation: This is the half-angle of the unit-circle boundary arc in the source parametrization. On the admissible density and angle domain, \(0<\alpha\leq\pi\).

classifications.informal_statement: The type-(B) exterior-circle radius is sin(β + arccos λ)/sin β.
classifications.latex_explanation: The common chord gives \(r\sin\beta=\sin\alpha\), so \(r=\sin\alpha/\sin\beta\). Admissibility for \(0<\lambda<1\) ensures the denominator is positive and the radius nonnegative.

classifications.informal_statement: The angular type-(B) weighted perimeter is 2((π − β)r + λα), with α = β + arccos λ and r = sin α/sin β.
classifications.latex_explanation: The exterior arc has length \(2r(\pi-\beta)\) and density one; the unit-circle arc has length \(2\alpha\) and density \(\lambda\). Their weighted sum is \(\mathsf P_{\mathrm B}(\beta)\).

classifications.informal_statement: The angular type-(B) weighted area is r²(π − β + sin β cos β) + α − sin α cos α − (1 − λ)π.
classifications.latex_explanation: The two chord segments have areas \(r^2S(\pi-\beta)\) and \(S(\alpha)\). Their sum is the Euclidean region area; subtract \((1-\lambda)\pi\) because the region contains the entire unit disk.

classifications.informal_statement: The angular type-(C) radius is 1/tan β.
classifications.latex_explanation: Orthogonality gives \(R=\cot\beta\) for \(0<\beta<\pi/2\). The total real formula is not interpreted as a finite geometric radius at either excluded endpoint.

classifications.informal_statement: The angular type-(C) weighted perimeter is 2(π − (1 − λ)β)/tan β.
classifications.latex_explanation: With \(R=1/\tan\beta\), subtract the density deficit \((1-\lambda)2R\beta\) of the inner arc from the full circumference \(2\pi R\). This is the source formula for \(\mathsf P_{\mathrm C}(\beta)\).

classifications.informal_statement: The angular type-(C) weighted area is (π − (1 − λ)(β − sin β cos β))/tan² β − (1 − λ)(π/2 − β − sin β cos β).
classifications.latex_explanation: The formula is \(R^2\pi-(1-\lambda)[R^2S(\beta)+S(\pi/2-\beta)]\), with \(R=\cot\beta\). The bracket is the overlap lens area, so the expression uses exactly the same density deficit as the geometric model.
